newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers set for EMU pact showdown in Dublin.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers set for EMU pact showdown in Dublin.

text.p: The failure of Germany and France to agree a budget pact that ensures fiscal discipline when Europe has a single currency has turned up the heat on EU finance ministers who meet in Dublin on Thursday.

While all EU members agree on the importance of curbing excessive spending inside a monetary union, the nuts and bolts of a mechanism that guarantees this objective has been one of the most contentious issues in planning a common currency.

Meeting in the German city of Nuremberg on Monday, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac highlighted just how difficult the negotiations have been by failing to settle differences over the proposed pact.

"French and German finance ministers are in the middle of important working groups and want to prepare a joint initiative and consult other European Union ministers before Thursday," Kohl told a news conference.

A political steer from the Franco-German gathering was anticipated by EU diplomats in order to set the stage for a compromise plan that would then be paraded at the European Council in Dublin this weekend.
But on Tuesday EU officials struck a cautious note, with some playing down the importance of agreement.
"Lack of an agreement would not prevent a progress report from going to the heads of state," said one EU official. "This is not the most important issue."

A delay in agreeing the pact does not necessarily affect the timetable for monetary union, due to be launched in 1999. But diplomats said that it would underline differences at a time when EU leaders want to send a strong message of unity both to their people and to financial markets.

Germany has found itself virtually isolated among EU nations on one specific aspect of the pact -- a strict numerical definition of "temporary and extraordinary" circumstances which would allow a nation to overshoot a maximum deficit level of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

Countries which run excessive deficits inside the monetary union -- over the three percent limit -- could face fines of up to a maximum of 0.5 percent of GDP, with an initial fine levied at 0.2 percent of output.
Bonn has argued that such a definition is needed to avoid loopholes that may be created by political compromise.
But others have protested against such a stringent approach, stressing that it would fail to take proper account of the economic differences among 15 members.

In essence, what the majority wants is a political process that evaluates a country's economic performance on a case-by-base basis, not a straightjacket that leaves political masters, in this case EU finance ministers, out of the decision-making process.

Summing up the standoff, Jaime Caruana, general director of the Spanish Treasury, told Reuters on Tuesday: "Germany wants clear rules, which is an interesting idea...At the same time we should take into account the history of economics (too)."
Should an accord on the stability pact remain elusive, work would continue next year with a view towards a resolution at the next EU summit, due in Amsterdam next June.

Apart from the budget pact, the ministers on Thursday will also concentrate their efforts on wrapping up a new European Exchange Rate Mechanism, known as ERM II, and the legal framework for a single currency.
On both fronts considerable progress has been made, with the outstanding issues viewed as relatively minor.

The expectation among Brussels-based diplomats is that a progress report on economic and monetary union will be ready for EU leaders to consider when they meet in Dublin castle on Friday and Saturday.
A political declaration by the leaders will then be issued with a clear emphasis on the points of agreement rather than the areas of discord.
